ei.title: The Mosquito: The Worst Bug on the Planet?
ei.subject: 공통영어2

fullPassage: PART 1 - THE NUISANCE You are on a camping trip with your family or friends. After a long day of hiking, you take a quick shower, sit in your favorite camping chair, pick up a soda, and let out a deep, contented sigh. Right at that moment, you hear that annoying and familiar buzzing sound. Beating its wings as fast as 600 times per second, a mosquito sneaks in and pierces your skin with its straw-like mouthparts. Next, it fills its belly with blood and then escapes quickly, leaving behind an itchy red bump. This is a mild allergic reaction to the mosquito’s saliva. The more you scratch the bump, the more it itches. But how do mosquitoes find their victims anyway? Carbon dioxide, which humans and other animals breathe out, is actually a key signal to mosquitoes that a nice meal is near. They are highly sensitive to CO₂ and can detect it from far away. That’s not the only cue they use to find their victims. When you sweat, you release certain chemicals that attract them. Moreover, they can easily notice that your body temperature has risen. Why do they want our blood in the first place? It turns out that only females bite us; they need protein to produce eggs. If our blood did not contain protein, they would not bother us. After the mosquito successfully takes a blood meal of up to three times her own body weight, she quickly lands on the nearest vertical surface. With the aid of gravity, she drains off the water from the blood she took. Using this concentrated blood, she develops her eggs over the next few days. She then lays roughly 200 floating eggs on the surface of a small pool of water. PART 2 - THE PREDATOR If you had to choose our greatest predator in nature, which would you pick? Sharks, lions, or bears? According to history professor Timothy Winegard, it is actually the mosquito. Mosquitoes can pass on deadly diseases like malaria and yellow fever. Over a million people worldwide die of these diseases every year. Throughout history, Winegard estimates that mosquitoes have killed more people than any other single cause — about fifty-two billion people, nearly half of all humans who have ever lived. Winegard claims that mosquitoes also played a role in shaping the history of several countries. Take the Roman Empire, for example. The fall of the Western Roman Empire was gradual, spanning over centuries. Here are commonly cited reasons for the fall of the empire: invasions by outside forces, economic troubles, and corruption. Diseases like malaria, however, also contributed. Rome, the capital of the empire, was once surrounded by a huge stretch of wetland. This was an ideal breeding ground for mosquitoes and hence a hot spot for malaria. On the one hand, mosquitoes helped protect the city against the armies coming to attack it. However, they eventually spread the disease not only throughout the city, but also throughout the empire, crushing much of the population. Here is another reason why Winegard considers the mosquito a powerful agent of historical change. In 1698, five ships set sail from Scotland, carrying twelve hundred settlers and valuable trade goods. They headed for the Darien region of Panama, where Scotland planned to create a trading center. After struggling through years of a food crisis, Scotland had hoped this would help raise its economic prospects. The ambitious plan, however, was brought down by the local diseases: yellow fever and malaria. Virtually no one from Scotland had ever encountered any of these diseases before. After six months, nearly half of them died, and the survivors returned to their ships and fled. If their immune systems had been much stronger, they would not have lost so many lives in such a short time. Surprisingly, human beings lived with and died of these diseases for thousands of years without understanding how they were spread. It was not until the end of the nineteenth century that we found out that mosquitoes spread malaria. Before this finding, no one imagined that these tiny annoying insects might be affecting our lives so deeply. Now we all know that human history is not free from the workings of the natural world. Read More Ladybugs and Earthworms ■ Ladybugs Ladybugs are probably the most well-known of all the helpful bugs in the garden. First of all, they eat quite a few of the bad bugs that prevent plants from growing. Each ladybug can eat fifty to sixty aphids per day and over five thousand in its lifetime. Their young eat aphids, too. If you grow plants that attract ladybugs, such as cilantro or mint, you may not have to worry about harmful bugs anymore. Even better, ladybugs can defend themselves by giving off a certain smell that their predators do not like. ■ Earthworms Earthworms are a great addition to your garden as well. They help keep your soil soft and breathable by digging tunnels that bring air to the roots of plants. They also eat the dead bits of plants that fall to the ground, recycling them back into the soil and helping new plants to grow. Moreover, their waste makes your soil richer, and they are excellent at breaking down organic matter in your garden. However, you should be careful about applying artificial fertilizers to your garden after introducing earthworms. They will find a new home when the soil around them changes.

questions.passage: Carbon dioxide, ①<u>what</u> humans and other animals breathe out, is actually a key signal to mosquitoes that a nice meal is near.  They are highly sensitive to CO₂ and can ②<u>detect</u> it from far away.  That’s not the only cue they use to find their victims.  When you sweat, you release certain chemicals that ③<u>attract</u> them.  Moreover, they can easily notice that your body temperature ④<u>has risen</u>.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.analysis:
❌ ① which → what: 선행사 Carbon dioxide를 받으며 콤마 뒤 계속적 용법에 쓰인 관계대명사 자리다. 관계대명사 what은 선행사를 포함하므로 이 자리에 올 수 없고 which가 옳다 ←정답
✅ ② detect: 조동사 can 뒤에 오는 동사원형으로 '탐지할 수 있다'는 구조로 적절
✅ ③ attract: 선행사 chemicals(복수)를 받는 주격 관계대명사 that의 동사로 수 일치가 맞아 적절
✅ ④ has risen: 주어 your body temperature(단수)에 맞춘 현재완료 has risen으로 적절
det.tip: 콤마+관계사의 계속적 용법에는 선행사를 포함하는 what을 쓸 수 없고, 선행사에 맞는 which를 씁니다.

questions.passage: Why do they want our blood in the first place?  It turns out that only females bite us; they need protein ①<u>to produce</u> eggs.  If our blood did not contain protein, they would not bother us.  After the mosquito successfully takes a blood meal of up to three times her own body weight, she quickly lands on the nearest vertical surface.  With the aid of gravity, she ②<u>drain</u> off the water from the blood she took.  ③<u>Using</u> this concentrated blood, she develops her eggs over the next few days.  She then ④<u>lays</u> roughly 200 floating eggs on the surface of a small pool of water.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① to produce: they need protein to produce eggs — '알을 낳기 위해'라는 목적을 나타내는 to부정사로 적절
❌ ② drain → drains: 주어 she(3인칭 단수)에 맞춰 동사도 drains가 되어야 한다. drain은 수 일치를 어겨 부적절 ←정답
✅ ③ Using: 주절의 주어 she와 능동 관계인 분사구문 Using this concentrated blood로 적절
✅ ④ lays: 주어 She(3인칭 단수)에 맞춘 현재시제 동사 lays로 적절
det.tip: 주어가 3인칭 단수(she)이면 현재시제 동사에 -s를 붙입니다(drains).

questions.passage: Virtually no one from Scotland ①<u>had ever encountered</u> any of these diseases before.  After six months, nearly half of them died, and the survivors returned to their ships and fled.  If their immune systems had been much stronger, they ②<u>would not have lost</u> so many lives in such a short time.  Surprisingly, human beings lived with and died of these diseases for thousands of years without ③<u>understand</u> how they were spread.  It was not until the end of the nineteenth century that we ④<u>found out</u> that mosquitoes spread malaria.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① had ever encountered: 기준 시점 이전의 경험을 나타내는 과거완료로 '결코 접해 본 적이 없었다'는 문맥에 적절
✅ ② would not have lost: If절이 had p.p.이므로 주절은 would have p.p. — 가정법 과거완료의 귀결절로 적절
❌ ③ understand → understanding: 전치사 without 뒤에는 명사 상당어구가 와야 하므로 동명사 understanding이 옳다. 동사원형 understand는 부적절 ←정답
✅ ④ found out: It was not until ... that 강조구문 속 과거시제 정동사로 적절
det.tip: 전치사(without) 뒤에는 동사원형이 아니라 동명사(V-ing)가 옵니다.

questions.passage: Rome, the capital of the empire, ①<u>was once surrounded</u> by a huge stretch of wetland.  This was an ideal breeding ground for mosquitoes and hence a hot spot for malaria.  On the one hand, mosquitoes helped protect the city against the armies ②<u>coming</u> to attack it.  However, they eventually spread the disease not only throughout the city, but also throughout the empire, ③<u>crushing</u> much of the population.  Here is another reason why Winegard considers the mosquito a powerful agent of historical change.  In 1698, five ships set sail from Scotland, carrying twelve hundred settlers and valuable trade goods.  They headed for the Darien region of Panama, ④<u>which</u> Scotland planned to create a trading center.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 어법상 틀린 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① was once surrounded: 주어 Rome이 '둘러싸인' 대상이므로 수동태 was surrounded로 적절
✅ ② coming: the armies를 뒤에서 수식하는 현재분사 coming to attack로 적절
✅ ③ crushing: 앞 절과 이어지는 분사구문 crushing much of the population으로 적절
❌ ④ which → where: 뒤에 완전한 절(Scotland planned to create a trading center)이 이어지고 선행사가 장소(the Darien region)이므로 관계부사 where가 옳다. 관계대명사 which는 부적절 ←정답
det.tip: 뒤에 완전한 절이 오고 선행사가 장소이면 관계대명사 which가 아니라 관계부사 where를 씁니다.

questions.passage: Beating its wings as fast as 600 times per second, a mosquito sneaks in and ①<u>pierces</u> your skin with its straw-like mouthparts.  Next, it fills its belly with blood and then ②<u>escapes</u> quickly, leaving behind an itchy red bump.  This is a ③<u>severe</u> allergic reaction to the mosquito’s saliva.  The more you scratch the bump, the more it itches.  But how do mosquitoes find their ④<u>victims</u> anyway?
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① pierces: 모기가 침 같은 주둥이로 피부를 '찌른다'는 문맥에 적절
✅ ② escapes: 피를 채운 뒤 재빨리 '달아난다'는 흐름에 적절
❌ ③ severe → mild: 가려운 붉은 자국 정도의 '가벼운(mild)' 알레르기 반응이라는 문맥이므로 severe(심한)는 정반대라 부적절 ←정답
✅ ④ victims: 모기가 '먹잇감(희생자)'을 찾는다는 문맥에 적절
det.tip: itchy red bump(가려운 붉은 자국) 정도라면 severe(심한)가 아니라 mild(가벼운) 반응입니다.

questions.passage: According to history professor Timothy Winegard, it is actually the mosquito.  Mosquitoes can pass on ①<u>deadly</u> diseases like malaria and yellow fever.  Over a million people worldwide die of these diseases every year.  Throughout history, Winegard estimates that mosquitoes have ②<u>killed</u> more people than any other single cause — about fifty-two billion people, nearly half of all humans who have ever lived. The fall of the Western Roman Empire was ③<u>sudden</u>, spanning over centuries.  Here are commonly cited reasons for the fall of the empire: invasions by outside forces, economic troubles, and corruption.  Diseases like malaria, however, also ④<u>contributed</u>.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 밑줄 친 ①~④ 중, 문맥상 낱말의 쓰임이 적절하지 않은 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① deadly: 말라리아·황열병 같은 '치명적인' 질병이라는 문맥에 적절
✅ ② killed: 모기가 어떤 원인보다 많은 사람을 '죽였다'는 문맥에 적절
❌ ③ sudden → gradual: 서로마 제국의 몰락이 수 세기에 걸쳐(spanning over centuries) 일어났다고 했으므로 '점진적인(gradual)'이 맞고 sudden(갑작스러운)은 모순이라 부적절 ←정답
✅ ④ contributed: 말라리아 같은 질병도 몰락에 '기여했다'는 문맥에 적절
det.tip: spanning over centuries(수 세기에 걸친)라는 단서로 보아 gradual(점진적인)이 알맞습니다.

questions.passage: But how do mosquitoes find their victims anyway?  Carbon dioxide, which humans and other animals breathe out, is actually a key signal to mosquitoes that a nice meal is near. questions.stem: 모기는 사람과 동물이 내뿜는 이산화탄소를 멀리 떨어진 곳에서도 감지할 수 있다.

det.analysis: T: 본문 'Carbon dioxide, which humans and other animals breathe out, is actually a key signal to mosquitoes...'와 'They are highly sensitive to CO₂ and can detect it from far away.'에서 모기가 사람·동물이 내뿜는 이산화탄소를 멀리서도 감지한다고 했으므로 진술은 참이다.
det.tip: can detect it from far away(멀리서 감지하다)가 근거입니다.

questions.passage: Why do they want our blood in the first place?  It turns out that only females bite us; they need protein to produce eggs.  If our blood did not contain protein, they would not bother us.
questions.stem: 사람을 무는 것은 수컷 모기이며, 수컷은 알을 만들기 위해 단백질을 필요로 한다.

det.analysis: F: 본문 'It turns out that only females bite us; they need protein to produce eggs.'에서 사람을 무는 것은 '암컷(females)'뿐이며 알을 만들 단백질이 필요한 것도 암컷이다. 진술은 '수컷'이라고 했으므로 사실과 다르다.
det.tip: only females bite us(암컷만이 사람을 문다)를 확인하세요.

questions.passage: Surprisingly, human beings lived with and died of these diseases for thousands of years without understanding how they were spread. Before this finding, no one imagined that these tiny annoying insects might be affecting our lives so deeply.
questions.stem: 모기가 말라리아를 옮긴다는 사실은 19세기 말에 이르러서야 밝혀졌다.

det.analysis: T: 본문 'It was not until the end of the nineteenth century that we found out that mosquitoes spread malaria.'에서 모기가 말라리아를 옮긴다는 사실이 19세기 말에 이르러서야 밝혀졌다고 했으므로 진술은 참이다.
det.tip: not until ~ (~에 이르러서야)이 밝혀진 시점을 나타냅니다.

questions.passage: Carbon dioxide, which humans and other animals breathe out, is actually a key __________ to mosquitoes that a nice meal is near.  They are highly sensitive to CO₂ and can detect it from far away.  That’s not the only cue they use to find their victims.  When you sweat, you release certain chemicals that attract them.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.analysis:
❌ ① obstacle(장애물): 이산화탄소가 모기에게 방해물이라는 것은 문맥과 반대라 부적절
✅ ② signal(신호): 이산화탄소가 '먹이가 가까이 있다'는 것을 알려 주는 핵심 '신호'이며 모기가 이를 감지한다는 흐름에 적절 ←정답
❌ ③ weapon(무기): 이산화탄소를 무기로 보는 것은 문맥과 무관해 부적절
❌ ④ disease(질병): 이산화탄소를 질병으로 보는 것은 의미가 통하지 않아 부적절
det.tip: cue(단서), detect(감지하다) 같은 표현이 signal(신호)을 암시합니다.

questions.passage: Rome, the capital of the empire, was once surrounded by a huge stretch of wetland.  This was an ideal __________ for mosquitoes and hence a hot spot for malaria.  On the one hand, mosquitoes helped protect the city against the armies coming to attack it.  However, they eventually spread the disease not only throughout the city, but also throughout the empire, crushing much of the population.
questions.stem: 다음 글의 빈칸에 들어갈 말로 가장 적절한 것은?

det.analysis:
❌ ① escape route(탈출로): 습지를 모기의 탈출로로 보는 것은 문맥에 맞지 않아 부적절
❌ ② hiding place(은신처): 은신처만으로는 '말라리아의 온상'이 되는 이유를 설명하지 못해 부적절
❌ ③ food source(먹이원): 습지가 모기의 먹이원이라는 근거는 본문에 없어 부적절
✅ ④ breeding ground(번식지): 습지대가 모기가 번식하기에 '이상적인 번식지'였고 그래서 말라리아의 온상이 되었다는 흐름에 적절 ←정답
det.tip: wetland(습지)와 hot spot for malaria(말라리아 온상)가 breeding ground(번식지)를 가리킵니다.

questions.stem: 위 글의 내용과 일치하지 않는 것은?

det.analysis:
✅ ① 본문 '600 times per second'로 초당 최대 600번 날갯짓한다고 했으므로 일치
✅ ② 본문 'This is a mild allergic reaction to the mosquito’s saliva'로 침에 대한 가벼운 알레르기 반응이라 했으므로 일치
✅ ③ 본문 'When you sweat, you release certain chemicals that attract them'으로 땀 속 화학물질에 이끌린다 했으므로 일치
❌ ④ 본문은 모기가 이산화탄소에 매우 민감하고 체온 상승도 감지한다고 했을 뿐, 이산화탄소보다 체온에 '더' 민감하다는 비교는 없으므로 불일치 ←정답
det.tip: 본문에 없는 '더 민감하다'는 비교급 진술을 만들어 낸 오답에 주의하세요.

questions.passage: PART 1 - THE NUISANCE You are on a camping trip with your family or friends.  After a long day of hiking, you take a quick shower, sit in your favorite camping chair, pick up a soda, and let out a deep, contented sigh.  Right at that moment, you hear that annoying and familiar buzzing sound.  Beating its wings as fast as 600 times per second, a mosquito sneaks in and pierces your skin with its straw-like mouthparts.  Next, it fills its belly with blood and then escapes quickly, leaving behind an itchy red bump.  This is a mild allergic reaction to the mosquito’s saliva.  The more you scratch the bump, the more it itches.  But how do mosquitoes find their victims anyway?  Carbon dioxide, which humans and other animals breathe out, is actually a key signal to mosquitoes that a nice meal is near.  They are highly sensitive to CO₂ and can detect it from far away.  That’s not the only cue they use to find their victims.  When you sweat, you release certain chemicals that attract them.  Moreover, they can easily notice that your body temperature has risen.  Why do they want our blood in the first place?  It turns out that only females bite us; they need protein to produce eggs.  If our blood did not contain protein, they would not bother us.  After the mosquito successfully takes a blood meal of up to three times her own body weight, she quickly lands on the nearest vertical surface.  With the aid of gravity, she drains off the water from the blood she took.  Using this concentrated blood, she develops her eggs over the next few days.  She then lays roughly 200 floating eggs on the surface of a small pool of water.  PART 2 - THE PREDATOR If you had to choose our greatest predator in nature, which would you pick?  Sharks, lions, or bears?  According to history professor Timothy Winegard, it is actually the mosquito.  Mosquitoes can pass on deadly diseases like malaria and yellow fever.  Over a million people worldwide die of these diseases every year.  Throughout history, Winegard estimates that mosquitoes have killed more people than any other single cause — about fifty-two billion people, nearly half of all humans who have ever lived.  Winegard claims that mosquitoes also played a role in shaping the history of several countries.  Take the Roman Empire, for example.  The fall of the Western Roman Empire was gradual, spanning over centuries.  Here are commonly cited reasons for the fall of the empire: invasions by outside forces, economic troubles, and corruption.  Diseases like malaria, however, also contributed.  Rome, the capital of the empire, was once surrounded by a huge stretch of wetland.  This was an ideal breeding ground for mosquitoes and hence a hot spot for malaria.  On the one hand, mosquitoes helped protect the city against the armies coming to attack it.  However, they eventually spread the disease not only throughout the city, but also throughout the empire, crushing much of the population.  Here is another reason why Winegard considers the mosquito a powerful agent of historical change.  In 1698, five ships set sail from Scotland, carrying twelve hundred settlers and valuable trade goods.  They headed for the Darien region of Panama, where Scotland planned to create a trading center.  After struggling through years of a food crisis, Scotland had hoped this would help raise its economic prospects.  The ambitious plan, however, was brought down by the local diseases: yellow fever and malaria.  Virtually no one from Scotland had ever encountered any of these diseases before.  After six months, nearly half of them died, and the survivors returned to their ships and fled.  If their immune systems had been much stronger, they would not have lost so many lives in such a short time.  Surprisingly, human beings lived with and died of these diseases for thousands of years without understanding how they were spread.  It was not until the end of the nineteenth century that we found out that mosquitoes spread malaria.  Before this finding, no one imagined that these tiny annoying insects might be affecting our lives so deeply.
